Lessons.Title: Attributes of Rectangles, Rhombuses, and Squares
ExplanationParagraphs: 2021 Grade3 Unit7 Lesson4 original local teacher lesson.html SHA256 6a7df9e955339cce5cc254693a2c4b844d487910572cc606ef11c60d3c687cd0 and preparation.html SHA256 72dd475d6b7fcbc51c31ec6ea8eae057a39d63e759b17c99e4f24e6154572246 were reviewed on the authorized device. The source title/activities and both original student-facing sections are mapped. The original independently formatted Student Task Statements PDF, publisher's visual files (including up to fourteen source figures/figure urls) and restricted Cool-down have not been pixel/page verified. No fabricated geometric letter answers from unseen shapes.

Warm-up Which One Doesn't Belong: More Attributes (10 minutes) has four source figures A–D. Source teacher synthesis explicitly says A, B and D are QUADRILATERALS (FOUR sides) and C is a TRIANGLE, while asking for at least one reason EACH original figure might be an outsider. Classification with teacher-checked reasoning admits multiple valid responses; do not hardcode only C as the unique possible odd one out.

Activity1 What Makes These Shapes So? (35 minutes): source starts by showing example vs NONEXAMPLE RIGHT TRIANGLES. Pupils circle qualifying shapes in ORIGINAL label set A–H, then answer what makes a right triangle. Public teacher launch explicitly says E in this set has a RIGHT ANGLE and is a right triangle, but other diagram classifications remain image-dependent and must not be guessed from the local alt-text index alone. A right triangle is a triangle that contains one right angle; a triangle cannot contain two right angles.

Activity1 continues with THREE distinct source quadrilateral families and original example/nonexample panels: RECTANGLES, RHOMBUSES and SQUARES. For EACH: first study examples and nonexamples, then CIRCLE all qualifying shapes in the corresponding publisher drawing set and EXPLAIN a characteristic that defines that class. The source does not ask one numerical count; each shape's correct membership is visual. Source teacher synthesis: a rectangle has four right angles (and equal opposite side lengths), a rhombus has all four sides equal, and a square has BOTH four equal sides and four right angles. A square therefore satisfies both rectangle and rhombus defining properties, though publisher preparation notes students may deepen this relationship in future lessons.

Class organization for activity: groups of TWO OR THREE. Teacher assigns each group ONE of rectangle, rhombus or square to analyze after launching right-triangle example with whole group; then groups SHARE with another group analyzing same shape and ask questions. Synthesis displays one labeled rectangle/rhombus/square poster, compares and contrasts their defining properties with teacher note of overlapping attributes. Offer rulers if side lengths are unclear and MLR8 partner sentence frames to reason about examples and nonexamples.

Original student tasks represent both INCLUDE and EXCLUDE decisions: do not accept superficially 'square-like' pictures without checking the four sides, four right angles or equality requirements. An angled/rotated square is still square if mathematical properties preserved. Do not claim any original letter in publisher 6-/5-shape sets belongs to a specific class without actual source figure visual inspection. Teacher-verified SOURCE E right triangle and A/B/D warm-up side counts are text evidence, NOT proof of pixel identical first-party art.

Teacher-gated publisher Cool-down Find the Rhombuses, independent pupil PDF, all source figures, actual grading UI, compiled .NET tests, CI, Stage D and academic approval remain UNVERIFIED. This first-party source-aligned explanation and rubric support teacher performance checks only.

KeyConcepts.Title: Right triangle
KeyConcepts.Definition: A triangle with one right angle.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Three sides; one angle shaped like the corner of a square.
KeyConcepts.Example: 2021 source teacher says sample E is a right triangle.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rectangle
KeyConcepts.Definition: A quadrilateral with four right angles; its opposite sides have equal length.
KeyConcepts.Example: A non-square rectangular shape with two longer and two shorter sides.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rhombus
KeyConcepts.Definition: A quadrilateral with four equal-length sides.
KeyConcepts.Rule: All four side lengths equal; right angles not required.

KeyConcepts.Title: Square
KeyConcepts.Definition: A quadrilateral with both four equal sides and four right angles.
KeyConcepts.Rule: square = rectangle AND rhombus by properties.
KeyConcepts.Example: A square rotated 45 degrees stays a square.

KeyConcepts.Title: Examples and nonexamples
KeyConcepts.Definition: Compare features shared by valid members and identify missing attributes in invalid shapes.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Explain WHY a source drawing is included/excluded.
KeyConcepts.Example: A four-equal-sided quadrilateral with no right angles is a rhombus but not a square.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original warm-up count
WorkedExamples.Question: Which of warm-up A–D are quadrilaterals?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use explicit source teacher textual note.
Steps: D has four sides; C is a triangle.
WorkedExamples.Check: Source also invites other odd-one-out explanations.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original right triangle example
WorkedExamples.Question: Why does source triangle E qualify?
Steps: E appears in source teacher's right-triangle examples.
Teacher note explicitly confirms E has right angle.
WorkedExamples.Check: Do not infer all other letter memberships without original figure.

WorkedExamples.Title: Rectangle vs rhombus vs square
WorkedExamples.Question: Can a shape have both rectangle and rhombus properties?
Steps: All four right angles makes it a rectangle.
All four equal-length sides makes it a rhombus.
Both together make it a square.
WorkedExamples.Check: Source promotes this inclusive understanding, not shape orientation.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Say every rhombus needs four right angles.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Rhombus requirement is all side lengths equal; slanted rhombuses need not be rectangles.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Separate equal sides and right angles.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Say squares are not rectangles because they look different.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Four right angles qualify a square as rectangle.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Classify original all figure letters from alt text without checking drawing.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Alt texts do not encode full side/right-angle geometry.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Teacher checks actual visual source figure.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat C as sole possible warm-up outsider.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Which One Doesn't Belong requests different justified choices.

SummaryPoints: Warm-up A,B,D are four-sided, C a triangle, but more than one valid outsider explanation.
Activity1 has right-triangle source example/nonexample, then rectangle, rhombus, square example/nonexample and independent original circle/explain subquestions.
Source right-triangle E verified by teacher text; other figure identities not fabricated.
Defining properties: triangle with right angle; rectangle four right angles; rhombus four equal sides; square both.
